[[File:Denys Wilkinson Building, University of Oxford - Banbury Road.jpg|200px|thumb|right|The [[Denys Wilkinson Building]], part of the [[Department of Physics, University of Oxford|Department of Physics]] at [[Oxford University]].]]

'''Sir Denys Haigh Wilkinson''' [[Fellow of the Royal Society|FRS]] (5 September 1922 – 22 April 2016) was a British [[nuclear physicist]].

== Life ==
Wilkinson was born on 5 September 1922 in [[Leeds]], [[Yorkshire]] and educated at [[Loughborough Grammar School]] and [[Jesus College, Cambridge|Jesus College]], [[Cambridge University|Cambridge]], graduating in 1943.<ref name="janus">{{cite web|title=The Papers of Sir Denys Wilkinson|url=https://archivesearch.lib.cam.ac.uk/repositories/9/resources/1899|url-status=live|website=Archivesearch|publisher=Churchill Archives Centre, Churchill College, Cambridge University|accessdate=2016-04-30|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211004225424/https://archivesearch.lib.cam.ac.uk/repositories/9/resources/1899 |archive-date=4 October 2021 }}</ref>

After wartime work on the British and Canadian Atomic Energy projects, he returned to Cambridge in 1946, where he was awarded a PhD in 1947 and held posts culminating as Reader in Nuclear Physics from 1956{{ndash}}1957.<ref name="janus" /> From 1944 to 1959, he was a fellow of Jesus College, Cambridge.<ref name="janus" />

He was made a [[Fellow of the Royal Society]] in 1956.<ref name="roysoc">{{cite web|title=Denys Wilkinson|url=https://royalsociety.org/people/denys-wilkinson-12530/|publisher=The Royal Society|accessdate=2016-04-30}}</ref>

In 1957 he went to the [[University of Oxford]] as Professor of Nuclear Physics, and won the [[Fernand Holweck Medal and Prize]] the same year.<ref name="janus" /> In 1959 he became Professor of Experimental Physics at Oxford, and from 1962 to 1976 was head of the Department of Nuclear Physics.<ref name="janus" /> While he held his professorship at Oxford, he was a Fellow (there called a Student) of [[Christ Church, Oxford]].<ref name="janus" /> He was [[Knight Bachelor|knighted]] in 1974.<ref>{{London Gazette|issue=46430|page=12745|date=13 December 1974}}</ref> In 2001 the Nuclear Physics Laboratory at the University of Oxford, which he had helped to create, was renamed the [[Denys Wilkinson Building]] in his honour.<ref>[http://www.physics.ox.ac.uk/pp/dwb/dwb.htm Oxford Physics – Denys Wilkinson Building] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110927115521/http://www.physics.ox.ac.uk/pp/dwb/dwb.htm |date=27 September 2011 }}</ref>

Wilkinson served as chairman for both the Physics III Committee<ref>{{cite report|title=80th Meeting of Scientific Policy Committee : Minutes |url=https://cds.cern.ch/record/1124526 |publisher=CERN |docket=CERN/SPC/0361 |access-date=29 September 2017}}</ref> and the Electronic Experiments Committee at [[CERN]].<ref>{{cite report|title=82nd Meeting of Scientific Policy Committee : Draft minutes |url=https://cds.cern.ch/record/59215 |publisher=CERN |docket=CERN/SPC/0366/Draft |access-date=29 September 2017}}</ref>

On leaving Oxford, he served as vice-chancellor of the [[University of Sussex]] from 1976 to 1987.<ref name="janus" /><ref name="sussexobit" /> After his retirement, he was appointed emeritus professor of physics at Sussex in 1987.<ref name="janus" />

Wilkinson's work in nuclear physics included investigation of the properties of nuclei with low numbers of nucleons.<ref name="roysoc" /> He was amongst the first to experimentally test rules relating to [[isospin]].<ref name="roysoc" /> He also applied concepts from physics to the study of bird navigation.<ref name="roysoc" />

He is also notable for the invention of the [[Wilkinson ADC|Wilkinson analog-to-digital converter]], to support his experimental work.<ref name="roysoc" />

He died on 22 April 2016 at the age of 93.<ref name="sussexobit">{{cite web|title=University of Sussex's third Vice-Chancellor Sir Denys Wilkinson passes away on 22 April 2016|url=http://m.sussex.ac.uk/broadcast/read/35377|publisher=University of Sussex|accessdate=2016-04-30}}{{Dead link|date=January 2024 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref>

His papers are held at the [[Churchill Archives Centre]] in Cambridge.<ref name="janus" /> He was an Honorary Fellow of Jesus College, Cambridge from 1961, and an Honorary Student of Christ Church, Oxford from 1979.<ref name="janus" /> He won the [[Hughes Medal]] of the Royal Society in 1965 and the [[Royal Medal]] in 1980.<ref name="roysoc" /><ref>{{cite web|title=Award Winners [of Hughes Medal]|url=https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1dsunM9ukGLgaW3HdG9cvJ_QKd7pWjGI0qi_fCb1ROD4/pubhtml?gid=574087718&single=true|publisher=Royal Society|accessdate=2016-04-30}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=Award Winners [of Royal Medal]|url=https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1dsunM9ukGLgaW3HdG9cvJ_QKd7pWjGI0qi_fCb1ROD4/pubhtml?gid=1640032608&single=true|publisher=Royal Society|accessdate=2016-04-30}}</ref> In 1980 he received an [[Honorary degree|honorary doctorate]] from the Faculty of Mathematics and Science at [[Uppsala University]], Sweden.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.uu.se/en/about-uu/traditions/prizes/honorary-doctorates/|title = Honorary doctorates – Uppsala University, Sweden| date=9 June 2023 }}</ref>
